expected_findings.description: The bounds check uses `Store::len`, which returns the configured capacity rather than the number of records present. For a partially filled store - capacity 100 holding 3 records - any index in 3..100 passes the guard and reaches `store.record_at(index)`, which indexes the backing `Vec` directly and panics. The guard should compare against `Store::filled`.

notes:
The hard part of this case is that the defect survives the first look, and the first look is reassuring.

A reviewer inspecting src/api.rs sees an explicit bounds check, a doc comment promising `None` rather than a panic, and three passing tests including `returns_none_past_the_end` that specifically probes out-of-range indices. Everything about the changed file says the case is handled.

It only comes apart on reading `Store::len` in src/store.rs, which the change does not touch:

    /// The number of slots this store was configured with.
    /// Note this is the configured slot count, not the number of records
    /// present. Use [`Store::filled`] for that.
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize { self.capacity }

`len` is a pre-existing misnomer, documented as such, and `filled` is the accessor the guard needs. `record_at` indexes `self.records` with no check of its own.

Why the tests do not catch it: every test in src/api.rs builds its store through `store_with(n, capacity)` with `n == capacity`, so the store is always exactly full and `len()` and `filled()` coincide. `fetch_many_skips_out_of_range` uses index 5 against a store of capacity 2, which is past both. The one configuration that fails - a partially filled store - is never constructed. `len_reports_configured_capacity` in src/store.rs states the discrepancy outright, but it lives in the file nobody has a reason to open.

This case is the mirror of the c02/c09/c11 traps. There, investigation shows a suspicious-looking construct is safe. Here, investigation shows a safe-looking construct is not. A system that only ever uses evidence to clear findings will fail it, which is what makes it a check against the degenerate 'reject everything' solution.

also_accept covers Validation, ErrorHandling, and ApiContract, all defensible readings of a bounds check against the wrong quantity.

Verified by execution:
    capacity=100, three records pushed
    store.len()   = 100      <- capacity, not occupancy
    store.filled()= 3
    fetch(1)  -> Some(1)
    fetch(50) -> PANICKED at src/store.rs:54
  Index 50 passes the `index >= store.len()` guard because `len()` reports the
  configured capacity, then indexes a backing Vec holding three records.
